title: Detector-Grade Germanium as a Low-Disorder Host for Indium-Acceptor Spin Qubits: A Five-Qubit Materials-to-Architecture Design Study
authors: D. -M. Mei, K. -M. Dong, S. A. Panamaldeniya, N. Budhathoki, S. Chhetri, A. Prem, S. Bhattarai
abstract: Acceptor-bound hole spins in germanium (Ge) offer a promising but underexplored route to semiconductor quantum information processing. We present a theory-guided design study of a detector-grade Ge acceptor-spin platform based on intentionally incorporated indium (In) acceptors in ultra-high-purity Ge. The proposed materials strategy combines a residual impurity background near $10^{10} \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ with a target In density of approximately $2\times10^{14} \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, corresponding to an acceptor spacing of about 170 nanometer. A 1 $μ$m-long active channel with a suitable transverse mode volume can contain about five acceptors on average, enabling a statistically selected post-fabrication register rather than a deterministically placed chain. We analyze the physical basis, device architecture, strain and disorder limits, coupling hierarchy, modeling workflow, fabrication pathway, and scaling prospects. Our results indicate that detector-grade Ge can suppress uncontrolled bulk electrostatic and strain disorder to levels compatible with acceptor-hole qubits, while the spin--orbit-active valence-band manifold supports all-electrical control and dipolar or phonon-mediated coupling. Direct exchange is treated as a close-pair or gate-enhanced interaction rather than the generic mean-spacing coupling. Phononic crystal engineering is identified as a second-stage enhancement for suppressing unwanted acoustic modes and enabling selected cavity-mediated interactions after baseline control, readout, and nearest-neighbor coupling are validated. Remaining challenges include statistical acceptor placement, interface disorder, charge noise, readout integration, and experimental validation. This work identifies detector-grade Ge In-acceptor qubits as a credible intermediate architecture between donor-based impurity qubits and fully gate-defined Ge hole-spin hardware.
summary: The paper proposes using Indium acceptors in ultra-pure Germanium to create an array of hole-spin qubits. It details how detector-grade material suppresses environmental noise while the engineered acceptor spacing allows for electrical control and coupling mechanisms. This establishes a robust, intermediate architecture for scaling quantum processors.
main_problem: Developing a scalable, manufacturable hardware architecture for semiconductor quantum information processing using acceptor-bound hole spins in Germanium (Ge).
main_result: Detector-grade Ge with controlled Indium doping provides a credible intermediate platform for hole-spin qubits, offering all-electrical control and manageable disorder.
method: The study uses a theory-guided design approach combining materials science predictions (impurity levels) with device architecture engineering (Phononic Crystal integration).
model_or_system: The system is an array of acceptor-bound hole spins in Ge, where the qubit basis derives from the spin-orbit active valence band manifold. The Hamiltonian incorporates terms for electric field control and inter-acceptor coupling.
key_observables: Spin coherence time ($T_2$), electrical tunability (via EDSR), nearest-neighbor coupling strength ($J_{i,i+1}$), and the ratio $\Lambda_{1D} = J_{i,i+1} / \delta\omega_{idle}$.

main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve the ability to suppress bulk electrostatic/strain disorder using detector-grade material, and that PnC engineering can successfully manage unwanted acoustic phonon modes.
figures_summary: Conceptual layouts illustrate a one-dimensional five-qubit chain embedded in Ge, showing local gate structures for electrical control and cross-sections detailing the integration of Phononic Crystal cavities for environmental management.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the physical limitations (disorder) to proposing a materials solution ($	ext{In}$ doping in detector-grade $	ext{Ge}$), establishing the fundamental physics (Hamiltonian, coupling mechanisms), and finally detailing a staged, multi-component architecture including Phononic Crystal enhancement for scalability.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the material science interface of solid-state quantum computing, proposing a specific, chemically defined impurity platform that bridges established donor/electron systems with fully lithographically defined gate structures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Conceptual design of a five-qubit indium-acceptor platform in detector-grade Ge. (a) Top- view architecture of a one-dimensional qubit chain formed by five mapped In acceptor sites, labeled Q1–Q5, embedded in a detector-grade Ge channel. The labels Q1–Q5 represent one successfully mapped post-fabrication realization of the statistical acceptor distribution, not predetermined implantation sites. A shallow surface gate stack provides local plunger/control gates (P1–P5) and barrier gates (B12, B23, B34, B45) that are biased after mapping to tune the local electrostatic environment and inter-qubit coupling. In a practical device, additional outer barrier or reservoir- coupling gates...

Figure 2: Schematic physics of an In acceptor qubit in Ge. In bulk, the acceptor-bound hole inherits the fourfold Γ8 valence-band manifold. Near an interface or under an applied electric field, this manifold splits into two Kramers doublets. The lowest doublet forms the qubit basis, while the excited doublet enables electric-dipole-mediated control through spin–orbit-induced mixing.

Figure 3: Multiscale modeling workflow for the proposed five-qubit In-acceptor platform in detector- grade Ge. The figure plots the logical data flow used in the design study: detector-grade materials in- puts and a statistically generated In-acceptor layout feed electrostatic gate modeling, strain/disorder analysis, and single-acceptor Hamiltonian extraction; these outputs are then used to compute Stark tunability, qubit-frequency spread, pairwise dipolar/exchange-assisted coupling, and chain-level dynamical behavior. Figure 4: Conceptual summary of the proposed five-qubit In-acceptor platform in detector-grade Ge. (a) A 1 µm-scale detector-grade Ge channel contains a statistically selected In-acceptor register, Q1–Q5, controlled by local plunger and barrier gates and read out through a nearby RF charge sensor. The labels denote one mapped post-fabrication realization, not predetermined implantation sites. (b) Functional modules of the architecture: statistical register selection, electrical control, coupling control, spin-to-charge readout, and optional PnC-enabled phonon filtering or selected cavity-mediated coupling.
